**2.**
Who, if not the other—myself, my own prisoner? Night flesh, the ear skewered by music in the open air, screams seeping well-deep to the root of the brain. Days of Treblinka, nights of guilt and viscera, the ferret pacing in my cage while sanity pools upon the floor.

**4.**
The sheer irrationality of it—the clamor of the mob, angels hewn from the block of darkness, a sunlit sky breaking through like shrapnel. Hard, screaming night; the feather-touch of troops improvising toward the kill. Panic, my enemy, my only handhold.

**5.**
Of the texture of elbows shattered and falls down stairwells, of hallucinated confessions rushing forth to stop the pain.

**6.**
Andean expanses of snow blind me; the flashlight of the Burglar of Death flares and lingers upon my eyes.

**7.**
In the Feast Halls, ghosts linger—feeding, evading the dogs and the memory of cracked bones.

**8.**
Present danger: colors hiss from a blue masque, bone-bonded. Autumn in no year's season, as a nerve twitches across the path.

**9.**

# Confronting Mortality and Memory

The text confronts the burdens of old age with unflinching honesty, depicting figures who stand "tagged and waiting" in line, their identities reduced to labels as they gaze toward the horizon at sundown. This image of waiting—patient, resigned, yet heavy with anticipation—establishes a meditation on the twilight of human life, where the setting sun mirrors the approach of an inevitable end.

Beyond the physical decline of age, the work delves into a deeper landscape of psychological imprisonment and trauma. It invokes the harrowing memories of Treblinka, summoning the specter of historical atrocity alongside more intimate experiences of torture. Here, sanity itself becomes fragile and unstable, described in visceral terms as something that "puddles the floor"—a mind dissolving, liquefying under the weight of unbearable recollection.

Memory and sickness intertwine throughout, refusing to remain separate. The speaker recalls the torturer's presence with disturbing immediacy, and this remembrance is accompanied by imagery of light and glacial cold that seems to drain the very air from the scene. The atmosphere grows thin and frozen, as though the act of remembering suffocates the present moment.

The imagery reaches its most frenetic pitch in capturing the irrationality and panic of violence. Troops appear "improvising for the kill," their brutality rendered chaotic and unpredictable rather than orderly. Hallucinations surge forward, rushing desperately to stop the pain—a psychological response to trauma so intense that the boundary between reality and delusion collapses entirely.

Presiding over all of this is death itself, rendered as an omnipresent and menacing figure: "the Burglar of Death," a thief who comes to steal life away. Ghosts linger in Feast Halls, haunting spaces that once held celebration but now echo with memories of "cracked bones" and the persistent sense of present danger. In this final vision, past and present, the living and the dead, converge in a single unsettling tableau where mortality is never distant and the horrors of memory remain perpetually alive.

# On the Fragmentation of Trauma: An Analysis

This text is a fragmented, surreal poem sequence exploring themes of aging, imprisonment, torture, and traumatic memory—evoked through references to Treblinka, torturers, and psychological disintegration—using disjointed imagery and stream-of-consciousness language.

The work refuses the conventions of linear narrative, instead assembling itself from broken pieces that mirror the shattered psyche it seeks to portray. Its structure enacts the very disorder it describes: sentences begin and dissolve, images bleed into one another, and time folds back upon itself so that past atrocities intrude upon a fragile present. The invocation of Treblinka anchors these abstractions in historical horror, transforming private suffering into a testament that reaches beyond the individual toward collective catastrophe. The figure of the torturer recurs like a haunting refrain, a presence that has colonized the speaker's inner landscape long after the physical infliction of pain has ended.

Aging appears here not as a natural process but as another form of imprisonment—the body becoming a cell that confines a mind already ravaged by remembered violence. The speaker inhabits a consciousness under siege, where the boundaries between then and now, between captor and captive, between self and annihilation, have grown porous and unreliable.

Through its distorted sensory impressions and collapsing perceptions of reality, the work powerfully conveys the enduring anguish of suffering and survival, illustrating how trauma fractures both memory and sanity.

What emerges is not merely a depiction of pain but an immersion in its aftermath. The reader is denied the comfort of distance; the disjointed language forces us to experience disorientation rather than simply observe it. Colors, sounds, and physical sensations arrive unmoored from their sources, suggesting a nervous system permanently altered by extremity. In this way, the poem argues that survival is itself a kind of continued wounding—that to endure is to carry the fracture within, to live perpetually in the ruins of a coherence that torture has made impossible. The fragmentation is thus both the subject and the method, and the poem's ultimate achievement lies in making legible the profound illegibility of a mind broken by human cruelty.

# Treblinka: History and Perpetrators

## What Was Treblinka?

Treblinka was one of the deadliest extermination camps established by Nazi Germany during the Holocaust. Located in occupied Poland, approximately 80 kilometers northeast of Warsaw, it operated primarily between July 1942 and October 1943. Unlike concentration camps designed for forced labor, Treblinka was built almost exclusively for one purpose: the systematic murder of human beings, primarily Jewish people from Poland and other parts of Europe.

## Who Were the Victims?

An estimated 800,000 to 900,000 people were killed at Treblinka, making it one of the sites of greatest loss of life during the Holocaust, second only to Auschwitz. The overwhelming majority of victims were Jews deported from the Warsaw Ghetto and other communities across Poland, as well as thousands of Roma people. Men, women, children, and the elderly were transported by rail under horrific conditions, often unaware of the fate awaiting them.

## Who Were the Perpetrators?

Treblinka was operated as part of **Operation Reinhard**, the Nazi plan to exterminate Polish Jews. The camp was run by a relatively small staff of German and Austrian SS officers, supported by auxiliary guards. Key figures included commandants such as **Franz Stangl**, who was later tried and convicted for his crimes. After the war, several perpetrators faced justice, though many escaped accountability for years or entirely.

## How Did It Operate?

The camp was engineered for rapid, industrialized killing. Victims arriving by train were deceived into believing they had reached a transit point, complete with a fake station designed to prevent panic. Within hours of arrival, most were murdered in gas chambers. The Nazis went to significant lengths to conceal their crimes, later attempting to dismantle the camp and disguise the site.

## Why Remember Treblinka?

In August 1943, prisoners staged an armed **uprising**, a remarkable act of resistance against overwhelming odds. Today, memorials stand at the site to honor the victims. Understanding *how* and *by whom* such atrocities were committed remains essential to preventing future genocide and preserving historical truth.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write 9 short surreal prose-poems about torture, imprisonment, aging, and trauma, using fragmented stream-of-consciousness language and disturbing imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
**I. The Clock That Ate My Hands**

They took the hours first. Peeled them like fruit. I counted the ceiling until the ceiling counted back and somewhere a faucet remembered my name, drip, drip, the syllables wearing thin—am I still the person who came in here or only the echo the walls kept for company. My wrists forgot their shape. The light bulb blinked morse code I never learned. Mother, the mattress has your smell, but mother has been dead for years, and years, and what is a year when it folds into itself like paper into a smaller and smaller crane.

---

**II. Inventory**

Item: one body, previously owned. Item: teeth, mostly. Item: a scream stored in the jaw for later, always for later. The men in the corridor speak in keys. I have become fluent in doors. When they close I am nowhere, when they open I am too much of somewhere. Somewhere is a chair with straps that know me better than lovers did. I gave them the truth and they wanted the other truth, the one that doesn't exist, so I built it, brick by brick, out of my own soft screaming.

---

**III. The Old Man Combs His Hair With a Fishbone**

Look how the mirror leaks. Every morning less of me arrives. My father lives in my knuckles now, cracking. The war I fought is fought again each night behind my eyelids, small men in small boats crossing the blood of my sleep. I am eighty. I am eight. The difference is a doorknob I can no longer turn. Grandchildren are noises in another room, sweet and impossible, like snow inside a bell. I outlived everyone who could have proven I was real.

---

**IV. Cell**

The window is a rumor. Grey feeds grey. I trained a spider and called it Sunday, called it Justice, called it the letter I will never receive. My handprint on the wall is aging faster than my hand. Somewhere a court is deciding whether I ever happened. The guard's boots are metronomes for a symphony of nothing. I have learned to eat memory. It is thin but it lasts. It tastes of my sister's kitchen, of a bicycle, of a version of the sky that had edges I could reach.

---

**V. What the Body Keeps**

You think you leave it in the room but the room comes home in you. Sits at the table. Uses your fork. There is a flinch that has outlived its reason, a hand rising to guard a blow that finished twenty years ago and never finished. The nervous system is an archive with no librarian. Touch me gently and the whole building floods. I am a house where all the alarms go off at the sound of kindness. Forgive the wiring. Someone crossed the wires in me on purpose, once, with pliers, humming.

---

**VI. Regarding the Number They Gave Me**

I had a name shaped like my grandmother's hands. Now I am a numeral sewn to a chest that rises and falls out of habit only. They subtract us. We are arithmetic in the mouth of the machine. At night the numbers whisper their old names to each other, a graveyard learning to speak. Mine slips further each dawn. If I forget it entirely will I finally be free or finally erased—the door and the wall wearing the same grey coat, laughing.

---

**VII. Aging Is a Slow Interrogation**

Where did you put it. Where did you put the running, the leaping, the wild wet laugh. Confess. The mirror has methods. The stairs have methods. Each joint a small official demanding papers I no longer have. My mother's face is arriving in mine like a ship long thought lost. She is asking me the same question the darkness asked: is this all. Is this all you brought back from the country of being young. And I open my hands, the fishbones, the empty, the tender ruined empty.

---

**VIII. Testimony**

Let the record show the ceiling. Let the record show the sound water makes inside a man. They wanted my confession, I gave them my childhood, they wanted a network, I gave them a spiderweb of every person who ever loved me, and I watched their faces fall from the walls of my memory one by one, apologizing. I am sorry, I told them, you were only ever a warmth I invented to survive the cold. The record shows nothing. The record was written in a language of bruises that fade even as you read them.

---

**IX. Release**

They open the last door and the world is enormous and wrong. Grass, unbearable. A child's balloon, obscene in its redness. I do not know how to be a man among the free—I flinch at mercy, I keep count of my own breathing, I have brought the cell with me, small and portable, folded behind my eyes. Somewhere in me a light bulb still blinks its morse. Somewhere the drip continues. I walk into the loud green shouting of the living, carrying my quiet, carrying my quiet, learning again the terrible weight of an unwatched sky.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a numbered series of experimental poetic fragments dealing with memory, madness, and violence, each with dense broken syntax and dark imagery like Treblinka, torturers, and the Burglar of Death.
counterfactuals.output:
**FRACTURES / a sequence**

**i.**
Memory the wet coal— I dig / dig / the tongue's
black shovel striking / nothing but the mothers'
teeth in Treblinka's throat, a rosary of
molars strung on nerve, and who / who counts them now
in the ash-arithmetic, the / long division of the smoke

**ii.**
The torturer keeps regular hours.
He waters his geranium at seven / kisses
the child's forehead / then / the electrodes hum
their domestic hymn. O ordinary hands, O
palms that pass the salt and break the / break the / break

**iii.**
I said to madness: sit. It sat.
It wore my father's coat and answered to
the wrong name, always the wrong name, the syntax
of the skull unhinged / a door that swings on
weatherless hinges into / no room / no room at all

**iv.**
Enter the Burglar of Death, soft-shoed,
picking the lock of the sternum with a
filed-down femur / lifting the small change of the
pulse / he takes / he always takes / the photographs first,
then the faces they were of, then the light that / saw them

**v.**
What the violence wanted was
grammar: a subject, a verb, a body
to receive the action / and it found me
conjugating in the dark— I struck, I strike,
I will have struck / the future perfect of the wound

**vi.**
Trainyards of the mind, and every boxcar
loaded / with a season I can't unremember—
the color of her dress before the dogs,
the smell of bread the day before / the day / before
the whistle / and the platform / and the not-arriving

**vii.**
Madness signs my letters now.
The penmanship is beautiful. It writes
to the dead and receives / replies / on stationery
of dried blood and pressed moth-wings, saying:
we are well here, we are / we are / we are

**viii.**
The Burglar returns for the remainder.
He has left me the exact weight of my
absence to carry / a suitcase full of the
sounds a house makes / cooling / after everyone
has gone / into the trees / into the numbered smoke

**ix.**
And still the shovel. Still the black coal glowing.
I dig toward a mercy shaped like forgetting
and strike / the teeth / the teeth / the small white teeth
that will not / will not / let the earth
close its enormous / merciful / mouth

---

Would you like me to extend the sequence, intensify the fragmentation, or push further into any single motif (the Burglar, the torturer's domesticity, the arithmetic of ash)?

# NINE SECTIONS FROM A FROZEN MOUTH

**i.**

snow arrives / unpermitted / on the tongues of dead artillery
white the color of no-more-thinking
sunlight a wound that will not / that cannot / that
who told the field it could keep breathing

**ii.**

mother in the ice again / mother in the ice again
her face a window nobody / built
i counted my hands wrong three winters running
the ghosts wear my old shoes and walk backward into the burning

**iii.**

blue hour / blue hour / soldiers folding into origami of themselves
here is the light that lies
here is the light that saws the head from the horizon
i have stopped believing in the difference between weather and grief

**iv.**

sanity a small dog running / smaller / smallest / gone under the drift
we sang the anthem of white erasure
teeth in the snow like alphabet nobody / assembles
the sun looked at me and I looked back and one of us went mad

**v.**

war is a color I taste when the frost speaks
speaks in the numbering of the missing
one two seven eleven zero zero zero
the ghosts are patient / the ghosts are patient / they have all my future in a jar

**vi.**

sunlight peeled from the day like skin from something warm once
snow eating the names off every stone
i wore my reason like a coat until the wind / until the wind unbuttoned
who is walking / who is walking through the mirror of the trench

**vii.**

they marched into brightness and became brightness
they marched into snow and became the argument snow was having
my mind a cathedral with no floor
falling / falling / and the light at the bottom is not light it is
teeth again / teeth in the drift again

**viii.**

ghost of my brother / ghost of my thinking / ghost of the ordinary morning
the field remembers being green the way I remember being sane
distantly / distantly / a rumor / a lie the body tells the body
snow snow snow the war-quiet / the after-quiet / the quiet that keeps score

**ix.**

and at the end the sun comes anyway / obscene / golden / not-caring
lays its gold across the ruined and the frozen and the almost-me
I am the last section of myself unmelted
say my name backward into the white
and watch even the ghosts / even the ghosts / look away

counterfactuals.output:
**Nine Fragments from the Hollow Wing**

**1.**
The wall has learned my name and keeps saying it wrong. Concrete sweats. I have counted the ceiling's teeth and there are more than there were, more than yesterday's mouth allowed, and the light that is not light comes sideways through the slot they forgot to seal, comes like water that has forgotten how to be wet. My hands. My hands are in the other room. Bring them.

**2.**
Boots. The corridor grows a spine of them, click into vertebra into click, and I make myself small as a swallowed thing. They open the door that is not a door. They ask questions with no words in them. I answer with a face I borrowed from a man who died against the far — against the far — I cannot finish the far.

**3.**
Mother's kitchen, but the ceiling is here. The bread is rising, rising, will not stop rising, floods the counter, floods the floor, dough at my ankles soft and warm as a wound, and she turns and her face is the guard's face is the wall's face is the mouth that says my name incorrectly. Eat, she says. It is Tuesday for the ninth week. It is Tuesday forever.

**4.**
They took the hours and stacked them somewhere I can hear. Drip. A metronome of somebody else's blood. I am fluent now in the dialect of the pipe, the long vowel of the vent, the consonant clatter when they drag the empty chair. I translate. Nobody. Nobody. The word for nobody is the same in every language they beat into me.

**5.**
Sun exists. I remember sun the way you remember a color from a language you no longer speak. There was a field. There was a field and a girl and the wheat went gold at the edge of — a field. I keep it in my molar so they cannot find it. When they hit me it flares like a struck match, gold, gold, gone.

**6.**
The mirror they gave me is water in a tin cup. I am ninety men in there, all of them thinning. My reflection has begun to disagree with my movements. It raises a hand I did not raise. It weeps on a schedule of its own. I no longer trust the thing that wears my face; it has been in the room longer than I have.

**7.**
Rats write on the floor in a script of small feet. Tonight the message says LEAVE and I laugh so hard the laugh becomes a color and the color becomes a shape and the shape sits in the corner and watches me until dawn, which does not come, which has been fired from its position, which sends a note of apology under the door in the handwriting of my father.

**8.**
When I close my eyes the sea is inside, but wrong, the tide going up not out, the waves standing vertical like people queued for something dreadful, patient, so patient, and I walk between them and each one is a day I did not survive though here I am, here I am, counting again, the ceiling's teeth, the more-than-yesterday, the mouth.

**9.**
And if I am freed — if the wall unclenches, if the boots forget their alphabet, if the bread stops — I will not know how to be a man in weather. I will bring the cell out in my chest like a stone swallowed young. Listen: they can open every door. The last one opens inward. The last one is my own hand, and my hands, you remember, my hands are still in the other room.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
